items.stimulus: Ornithologist Hanne Vik spent three summers tracking Arctic terns that nest on a remote northern island. Most of the birds she tagged were between four and twenty years old, but the oldest, a female first banded as a chick, was 31 when Vik recaptured her. Terns typically begin breeding at about age three, and few are thought to keep breeding past their mid-twenties. The 31-year-old bird, however, was still raising chicks, a fact that surprised Vik even more than the bird's age.
items.stem: According to the text, what surprised Vik?
choices: That the oldest tern she recaptured was still raising chicks
That most of the terns she tagged were between four and twenty
That terns typically begin breeding at about three years of age
That a tern first banded as a chick could ever be recaptured
items.explanation: The last sentence answers the question directly: the 31-year-old bird 'was still raising chicks, a fact that surprised Vik.' Choice A restates that sentence.

B.why: The passage does say this about the age range, but it is background information. Nothing says the range surprised Vik. You chose a true detail that answers a different question.

C.why: This is a general fact about terns that the passage gives as context. The text never says it surprised Vik. You matched words from the passage without checking that they answer 'what surprised.'

D.why: The passage mentions that the bird was banded as a chick and later recaptured, but it never says the recapture itself was surprising. You added a reaction the text does not state.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: In a survey of 140 school cafeterias, nutrition scientist Rosa Imbert found that most lunches met federal limits on sodium and saturated fat. Her concern lay elsewhere: fewer than a third of the meals contained enough fiber, a nutrient linked to steady energy and healthy digestion in children. Imbert has proposed that schools replace refined grains with whole-grain versions, a change she estimates would cost districts very little. She also recommends adding beans to at least two lunch menus each week.
items.stem: According to the text, why was Imbert concerned about the school lunches?
choices: Most of the lunches exceeded federal limits on sodium and fat.
Fewer than a third of the lunches contained enough fiber.
Schools could not afford to switch to whole-grain foods.
Beans appeared on fewer than two lunch menus each week.
items.explanation: The sentence beginning 'Her concern lay elsewhere' answers the question: fewer than a third of the meals had enough fiber. Choice B restates it.

A.why: The passage says most lunches met the sodium and fat limits. You picked up the words 'sodium' and 'fat' and reversed what the text says about them.

C.why: Whole grains come up in Imbert's proposed solution, and she estimates the switch would cost 'very little.' You treated the proposed fix as the cause of her concern and flipped her cost estimate.

D.why: Imbert recommends adding beans to two menus a week, but the passage never says how often beans currently appear. You turned a recommendation into a finding the text does not report.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: Most studies of how much ride-hailing drivers work have relied on surveys in which drivers estimate their own weekly hours. Labor economist Dev Anand suspected that such estimates ran high. So rather than asking drivers, he analyzed four million trip records supplied by a ride-hailing company. The records showed that drivers worked an average of 19 hours per week, about six fewer than survey respondents in earlier studies had reported.
items.stem: According to the text, how did Anand's approach differ from that of other researchers?
choices: He analyzed trip records instead of asking drivers for estimates.
He found that drivers worked an average of 19 hours per week.
He surveyed drivers directly about the hours they worked weekly.
He studied drivers who worked six more hours than the average.
items.explanation: The passage contrasts surveys of drivers with Anand's choice to analyze 'four million trip records' 'rather than asking drivers.' Choice A describes that difference in method.

B.why: This is Anand's result, not his approach. The question asks how his method differed, and you answered with what the method found.

C.why: Surveys are what other researchers used. Anand deliberately avoided them. You gave Anand the approach that belongs to the other researchers.

D.why: The number six is the gap between survey reports and Anand's finding. It does not describe a group of drivers he studied. You took a number from another part of the passage and attached it to the wrong thing.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: In 2022, health officials in the city of Arlen faced a rise in measles cases concentrated in two neighborhoods. During earlier outbreaks, the city had opened a single central clinic. This time, officials sent mobile vaccination vans to schools and markets in the affected areas. Within six weeks, vaccination rates in those neighborhoods rose from 81 percent to 93 percent. Officials credit the vans' convenience, though they note that a radio campaign running at the same time may also have helped.
items.stem: According to the text, what did officials in Arlen do in response to the 2022 rise in measles cases?
choices: They opened a single central clinic to serve the entire city.
They sent mobile vaccination vans into the affected areas.
They raised vaccination rates in every neighborhood to 93 percent.
They ran a radio campaign in place of offering vaccinations.
items.explanation: The sentence beginning 'This time' says officials 'sent mobile vaccination vans to schools and markets in the affected areas.' Choice B restates that sentence.

A.why: The central clinic was the city's response to earlier outbreaks. The 2022 approach was set up as a contrast to it. You took a detail from the wrong time period.

C.why: The 93 percent figure applies only to the two affected neighborhoods. You took a real number from the passage and applied it to every neighborhood in the city.

D.why: The radio campaign ran alongside the vans and did not replace vaccination. You took a secondary detail and made it the main response.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: For centuries, mapmakers filled unexplored regions with features they had never seen. For example, an 1804 map by cartographer Elias Marten showed a large lake, which he named Lake Sorrel, at the center of an inland plateau. Marten never visited the plateau. Instead, he relied on a trader's secondhand account of the region. Later mapmakers copied the lake onto their own maps for decades. Not until 1871 did a survey team cross the plateau, and it found only dry grassland where the lake was supposed to be.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Marten base his depiction of Lake Sorrel on?
choices: A trader's secondhand account of the region
His own visit to the center of the plateau
A survey team's crossing of the plateau
Maps drawn by other mapmakers of the time
items.explanation: The text says Marten 'relied on a trader's secondhand account of the region.' Choice A matches that line.

B.why: The passage states plainly that Marten 'never visited the plateau.' You chose the opposite of what the text says.

C.why: The survey team crossed the plateau in 1871, decades after Marten's map, and showed that the lake did not exist. You used a detail from a later part of the passage that answers a different question.

D.why: In the passage, other mapmakers copied Marten, not the other way around. You reversed the direction of the copying.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: Seismologists can estimate how often large earthquakes strike a fault by studying layers of sediment that past quakes have disturbed. At Corran Marsh, geologist Ama Owusu dug a trench across the Tessel Fault and found evidence of five major earthquakes. Using radiocarbon dating, she determined that the sediment layers in the trench spanned roughly 2,400 years and that the oldest of the quakes struck about 2,100 years ago. The most recent, she concluded, occurred around 340 years ago.
items.stem: According to the text, approximately how long ago did the oldest earthquake Owusu identified occur?
choices: 340 years
480 years
2,100 years
2,400 years
items.explanation: The text says 'the oldest of the quakes struck about 2,100 years ago.' Choice C matches that number.

A.why: 340 years is the date of the most recent quake, not the oldest. You picked up a number from the next sentence.

B.why: You got 480 by dividing 2,400 years by five quakes. The passage never does this calculation, and the result is not the age of any quake. You reasoned past what the text actually says.

D.why: 2,400 years is how long the sediment layers span. It is the outer limit of the record, not the age of the oldest quake. You confused a range boundary with the specific figure the question asks for.

items.stimulus: Musicologists have long attributed the Lindqvist Partbooks, an anonymous set of sixteenth-century choral manuscripts, to a single monastery scribe. However, a recent study by musicologist Clara Hesse found three distinct styles of handwriting in the books, along with two different types of paper. Hesse concludes that the partbooks were likely copied by several scribes over a period of years rather than by one person working alone.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Hesse find in the Lindqvist Partbooks?
choices: Three distinct styles of handwriting
The name of a single monastery scribe
Choral music composed by several scribes
Paper that was all produced in one year
items.explanation: After 'However,' the text says Hesse 'found three distinct styles of handwriting in the books.' Choice A matches that line.

B.why: The partbooks are anonymous. The single-scribe idea is the older view that Hesse's study challenges, not something she found. You took the view set up before 'However' and treated it as her finding.

C.why: Hesse concludes that several scribes copied the music. She says nothing about who composed it. You changed 'copied' into 'composed,' which is a claim the text never makes.

D.why: Hesse found two different types of paper and concludes that the copying took place 'over a period of years.' You chose the opposite of what she found.

items.stimulus: Musicologists long assumed that the lute songs in a manuscript from the 1590s, now held in Leiden, were copied by a single scribe, since the handwriting looks uniform throughout. However, when researcher Ilse Brandt analyzed the ink, she found that the songs on the final twelve pages were written in an iron-gall ink that appears nowhere in the earlier pages. She concluded that a second copyist had added those songs later.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Brandt conclude that a second copyist had worked on the manuscript?
choices: The handwriting on the final pages differed from the rest.
The ink on the final pages differed from the earlier ink.
The handwriting looked uniform across the whole manuscript.
The final pages were dated to a later decade than the rest.
items.explanation: The question asks why Brandt reached her conclusion, so find the sentence about what she found. It says the songs on the final twelve pages used an iron-gall ink that 'appears nowhere in the earlier pages.' items.stimulus: Radiocarbon dates from a hearth at the Kestrel Cove site on the Oregon coast fall between 9,800 and 10,600 years ago. Archaeologists note that most hearths in the region were used for only a few seasons before being abandoned. However, a series of layered clay floors beneath this hearth suggests that it was rebuilt again and again. The excavation team estimates that people returned to it over roughly 400 years.
items.stem: According to the text, for about how long did people keep returning to the hearth at Kestrel Cove?
choices: Only a few seasons
Roughly 800 years
Roughly 400 years
Roughly 10,600 years
items.explanation: The question asks how long people kept returning, so find the sentence about returning. The last sentence says the team 'estimates that people returned to it over roughly 400 years.' Choice C matches it directly. You don't need to calculate anything.

A.why: 'A few seasons' describes most other hearths in the region. The 'However' sentence sets this hearth apart from them. You gave a detail about the wrong hearths.

B.why: You subtracted 9,800 from 10,600 and treated the gap between the dates as the period of use. The text never says this. It states a separate estimate of 400 years. Don't reason past the sentence that answers the question.

D.why: 10,600 is one end of the range of radiocarbon dates. It tells you how long ago the hearth was used, not how long people kept coming back to it. You picked a number from the passage that answers a different question.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: In 2019, health officials in a small coastal town noticed that cases of stomach illness at the local primary school had doubled in a single winter. They traced most of the cases to the school's shared water fountains. To slow the spread, they placed hand-washing stations beside every fountain. By the following winter, cases at the school had fallen by half.
items.stem: According to the text, what did health officials trace most of the illness cases to?
choices: The shared water fountains at the school
The hand-washing stations beside the fountains
A shortage of soap in the school's washrooms
The cold winter weather in the coastal town
items.explanation: The question word is 'traced to', so find the sentence that says what the cases were traced to: 'They traced most of the cases to the school's shared water fountains.' Choice A puts that sentence in other words. This groundwork prepares you for 'According to the text' detail questions on the test, where you have to find the one sentence that answers the question before you look at the choices.

B.why: The hand-washing stations do appear in the text, but they are the fix officials put in place, not the cause they found. You used the solution as the answer to a question about the cause, which is exactly what this question type is built to catch.

C.why: The text never says the school was short of soap. Because the solution involved washing, you assumed the cause must have been a lack of washing, but no sentence says so.

D.why: The text mentions a coastal town and winter, but it never blames the weather. You built a cause out of setting details. Try to put your finger on the line that proves it. You won't find one.

items.stimulus: Sports scientists timed 40 runners, aged 18 to 30, over a short sprint on two separate days. On one day the runners sprinted with no warm-up; on the other they first completed a 12-minute warm-up. After the warm-up, their sprint times improved by 4 percent on average. In a follow-up trial, warm-ups longer than 20 minutes produced no further gain.
items.stem: According to the text, by how much did the runners' sprint times improve after the 12-minute warm-up?
choices: 4 percent
12 percent
20 percent
30 percent
items.explanation: Find the sentence about the improvement: 'After the warm-up, their sprint times improved by 4 percent on average.' That number answers the question, so the answer is 4 percent. On the test, detail questions often put every number from the passage in the choices. This drill trains you to match the number to the question word, here 'improve by how much', and not just to any number you remember from the passage.

B.why: 12 is the length of the warm-up in minutes, not the size of the improvement. You took a number from the right sentence area, but it answers a different question: how long the warm-up lasted.

C.why: 20 comes from the follow-up trial. It is the warm-up length after which there was no further gain. It is a cut-off for time spent warming up, not the improvement in sprint times.

D.why: 30 is the upper end of the runners' age range. It is the top of a range in the passage, not a result. Every number in these choices appears in the text, but only one answers this question.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: Many people assume that a river's spring flood is driven mainly by rain. In the Halvern Valley, however, hydrologists found that about 70 percent of the river's spring flow comes from snow melting high in the surrounding mountains. Rain supplies most of the remaining water, while groundwater seeping in from the valley floor adds only a small share.
items.stem: According to the text, what supplies most of the Halvern River's spring flow?
choices: Snow melting in the mountains
Rain falling during the spring
Groundwater from the valley floor
Water released from valley lakes
items.explanation: The sentence after 'however' gives the finding: about 70 percent of the spring flow 'comes from snow melting high in the surrounding mountains.' Seventy percent is most of the flow, so the answer is snowmelt. This drill prepares you for detail questions in passages that set up a common belief and then correct it. The answer comes from what follows the pivot word, not from the belief stated before it.

B.why: Rain is what 'many people assume', and the text then corrects that belief. Rain does supply 'most of the remaining water', but that is most of the leftover 30 percent, not most of the total. You stopped reading at the familiar word 'most' and missed what it was attached to.

C.why: The text says groundwater adds 'only a small share', which is the opposite of most. You picked a source the passage mentions but gave it a larger role than the passage does.

D.why: The text never mentions lakes. You may have used what you already know about rivers in place of what this passage says. Go back and point at the line, and you won't find one.

items.stimulus: In a survey of 500 warehouse workers, most said that, given the choice, they would take higher hourly pay over a shorter working week. Workers with young children were the exception: a majority of them said they would prefer a four-day week. The researchers suggest that, for some workers, schedules may matter as much as wages.
items.stem: According to the text, how did workers with young children differ from most other workers in the survey?
choices: They were more likely to prefer a four-day week.
They were more likely to prefer higher hourly pay.
They were more likely to rank schedules above wages.
They were more likely to take part in the survey.
items.explanation: The question asks how one group differed, so find the sentence that marks the difference: 'Workers with young children were the exception: a majority of them said they would prefer a four-day week.' Choice A restates it. On the test, 'how did X differ from others' questions put the other group's behaviour in the choices too. This drill trains you to check which group each choice describes.

B.why: Preferring higher hourly pay is what most of the other workers said. You gave the parents the majority's answer, which is the opposite of how the text says they differed.

C.why: This comes from the researchers' final sentence, but that sentence is hedged ('suggest', 'may') and says schedules may matter 'as much as' wages, not more. The workers themselves never ranked schedules above wages. You turned a careful suggestion into a stronger claim.

D.why: The text says nothing about which workers were more likely to respond to the survey. The words 'survey' and 'workers' come from the passage, but the claim about them does not.

She used thick steel reinforcement to keep the concrete deck from cracking.

items.stimulus: Farmers have long assumed that weed seeds buried by plowing lose their ability to sprout within a few years. The seeds had lost their ability to sprout within a few years of burial.
Seeds buried at 20 centimeters sprouted more often than shallower seeds.
Plowing had completely eliminated velvetleaf from the plots she studied.

The congregation that used it was founded in the 1790s.

items.stimulus: Slow-slip events, in which a fault moves over days or weeks rather than seconds, release built-up energy without producing strong shaking. Seismologist Kenji Arai found that along Japan's Nankai Trough, such events recur roughly every six months. Some observers have described them as a harmless way for faults to let off pressure. However, Arai cautions that slow slip may also add stress to neighboring locked sections of the fault, which could make a large earthquake there somewhat more likely.
items.stem: According to the text, which of the following is NOT stated about slow-slip events?
choices: They unfold over a span of days or weeks.
They recur about twice a year at the Nankai Trough.
They may add stress to nearby locked fault sections.
They reliably prevent large earthquakes on the fault.
items.explanation: The text never says slow-slip events prevent large earthquakes. After "However," Arai warns that they may make a large earthquake somewhat more likely. The idea of "letting off pressure" belongs to "some observers," and the text sets that view up only to correct it. So this choice is the one that is not stated.

A.why: The first sentence says the fault moves "over days or weeks rather than seconds." This is stated, so it can't be the answer to a NOT question. You picked a true statement.

B.why: "Roughly every six months" means about twice a year, so this is stated in different words. If you rejected it because the wording doesn't match, convert the number before you decide. The text does support it.

C.why: This paraphrases Arai's caution that slow slip "may also add stress to neighboring locked sections." It is true, and it even keeps the hedge word "may," so it is not the exception.

items.stimulus: Fiber is often credited for the heart benefits of whole oats. But nutrition scientist Priya Nair's team points to avenanthramides, compounds found in no other common cereal grain. In a twelve-week trial with 90 adults, participants who ate oat bran rich in these compounds showed lower markers of blood-vessel inflammation than those who ate oat bran with the compounds removed. Because both groups consumed the same amount of fiber, the difference likely came from the avenanthramides themselves.
items.stem: According to the text, which of the following is NOT true of the trial Nair's team conducted?
choices: It ran for a period of twelve weeks.
It enrolled a total of 90 adults.
Its two groups ate equal amounts of fiber.
It compared oats with other cereal grains.
items.explanation: In the trial, both groups ate oat bran. One group's bran had avenanthramides and the other group's had them removed. No other grain was tested. The words "other common cereal grain" come from an earlier sentence, which explains what is special about the compounds. That sentence doesn't describe the trial, so this choice is not true of the trial.

B.why: The text says the trial had "90 adults," so this is stated directly. In a NOT question, a choice you can point to in the text is a choice to eliminate.

items.stimulus: Public health officials often credit hand-washing posters for declines in hospital infections. However, a review of twelve regional hospitals by epidemiologist Rana Okafor points elsewhere. In wards that added only posters, infection rates fell by 4 percentage points over two years. In wards that also installed sanitizer dispensers beside every bed, rates fell by 19 percentage points over the same period. Okafor concludes that convenience, more than reminders, likely did most of the work.
items.stem: According to the text, how much larger was the drop in infection rates in wards with bedside dispensers than in wards with posters alone?
choices: 12 percentage points
15 percentage points
19 percentage points
4 percentage points
items.explanation: The question asks about the gap between two groups. The text says rates fell by 19 percentage points in the dispenser wards and by 4 in the poster-only wards. 19 minus 4 is 15, so the dispenser wards' drop was 15 percentage points larger.

A.why: You took 12 from somewhere else in the passage. It is the number of hospitals Okafor reviewed, not a change in infection rates, so it answers a different question.

C.why: 19 is how much rates fell in the dispenser wards alone. The question asks how much larger that drop was than the poster-only drop, so you still need to subtract the 4.

D.why: 4 is how much rates fell in the poster-only wards. You answered about one group when the question asks for the difference between the two.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: Hydrologists can estimate how long water has been underground by measuring trace gases that dissolved in it when it last touched the air. In a recent survey of a desert aquifer, a research team sampled two wells. Water from a shallow well, 30 meters deep, had been underground for roughly 60 years. Water from a deep well, 300 meters down, was roughly 900 years old. The team warns that such old water may refill far more slowly than pumping removes it.
items.stem: According to the text, how much older was the water from the deep well than the water from the shallow well?
choices: 270 years
900 years
840 years
60 years
items.explanation: The text gives the shallow-well water an age of roughly 60 years and the deep-well water an age of roughly 900 years. The gap is 900 minus 60, which is 840 years.

A.why: 270 is the difference in the wells' depths (300 meters minus 30 meters), not in the water's age. You used numbers from a different sentence to answer a question about time.

B.why: 900 years is how old the deep-well water is. The question asks how much older it is than the shallow-well water, so you answered about one quantity, not the difference.

D.why: 60 years is the age of the shallow-well water. That is one side of the comparison, not the difference between the two ages.

items.subtype_name: According to the text, what is stated
items.stimulus: Road salt corrodes the steel bars inside concrete bridge decks, which shortens their lives. For example, the original deck of the Millbrook Bridge, built in 1971 with steel reinforcement, needed major repairs after 22 years. When the county replaced that deck in 2004, engineers used glass-fiber bars instead. Inspectors in 2024 found that the new deck, then 20 years old, showed no corrosion. Engineers now project that it will go 75 years before needing major repairs.
items.stem: According to the text, how many more years before major repairs do engineers project for the fiber-reinforced deck than the original deck lasted?
choices: 53 years
33 years
75 years
20 years
items.explanation: The original steel-reinforced deck needed major repairs after 22 years. Engineers project the fiber-reinforced deck will go 75 years. The gap is 75 minus 22, which is 53 years.

B.why: 33 is the time between the two construction dates (2004 minus 1971). Both numbers appear in the passage, but they measure when the decks were built, not how long they last before major repairs.

C.why: 75 years is the projected life of the fiber-reinforced deck alone. The question asks how much longer that is than the original deck lasted, so you still need to subtract the 22.

D.why: 20 years is how old the new deck was at the 2024 inspection. That number comes from a different sentence and is not a difference between the two decks' service lives.
